## Where This Fits
**Every model in Weeks 7–9 assumed that the audio coming in is the user's speech. This week removes that assumption.** A system that listens while it speaks receives a sum at its microphone: the user's voice, plus **the system's own voice coming back through the room** (the waveform that Weeks 8–9 generated is now a term on the input side), plus other people nearby, plus noise. A half-duplex system sidesteps the largest of those terms because it does not listen while talking. A full-duplex system cannot — and the moment it cares about most, the user barging in, is exactly the moment all four terms are present at once. One question runs through the week: **for each term in the microphone signal, on what grounds can we remove it — and once it is removed, what is left behind, and who pays for it?**

"On what grounds" is what turns five seemingly unrelated topics into one line. Every module relies on a kind of **side information**. (1) **Voice activity detection** removes nothing; it only answers "is anyone speaking in this frame", relying on speech and noise being statistically different. (2) **Acoustic echo cancellation** removes the system's own voice using the strongest side information in the whole course — the **reference signal is known** — which makes it a system-identification problem rather than a separation problem. (3) **Enhancement** removes noise with no reference at all, relying on a prior over what speech looks like: statistical assumptions, then learned masks, then generative models. (4) **Beamforming** relies on space: a second microphone adds a dimension that is independent of the spectrum. (5) **Separation** has no side information, which is why it can pull voices apart but cannot say which output is whom (the permutation problem). (6) **Target speaker extraction and speaker verification** rely on an enrollment utterance, replacing "pull apart" with "find this person". Finally, (7) **diarization and "was that addressed to me?"** push the problem from the signal to the edge of the dialogue, which is where Week 12 picks it up. The weaker the side information, the more a model has to lean on its prior — and the less natural the residue it leaves.

"What is left behind" is the week's central correction and one of the six core failure cases of the course: **after enhancement, SNR and PESQ go up, and the word error rate can go up too.** The mechanism has a name. Enhancement error splits into residual noise and **artifacts** — the part of the output that cannot be written as a linear combination of the speech and the noise, i.e. what the nonlinear processing itself created and the downstream model never saw in training. This is Week 9 in a different place: SNR, PESQ and SI-SDR are *judges*, an optimised judge has blind spots, and the real downstream consumer (the recogniser, Week 9's spoofing detector, Week 12's turn-taking model) is a different judge. Linear processing — the linear filter in an echo canceller, a beamformer — creates almost no artifacts, which is the common reason behind two practical conventions: a linear echo canceller first with a neural network only for the residual, and "let the network estimate the mask, let a linear filter do the removing". Generative enhancement brings Week 7's hallucination to the front end: when the evidence is weak the output follows the prior, and it sounds clean while containing a phoneme the user never said.

On the three course axes. **Representation:** this is the only week that stays entirely in front of the tokens — waveforms and the complex STFT — and phase returns (a mask applied to a noisy STFT generally does not give the STFT of any signal; Week 2's consistency). **Latency:** two cells are filled in — the front end's algorithmic delay (one STFT frame plus look-ahead) and the VAD hangover, which lands directly in the "endpoint detection" cell of Week 1's response budget; and the first term of Week 1's *stop* budget, barge-in detection, is physically a VAD placed after the echo canceller. If the canceller has not converged, what the system hears is itself, and it interrupts itself. **Supervision:** an adaptive filter has no training phase at all — its weights are updated sample by sample in use, with the error signal as teacher — while neural enhancement and separation are trained on *synthetic pairs* (clean speech plus noise; the label is free), at the price of a gap between simulated and real recordings.

For the local languages, three points of different strength. The front end operates on signals and is language-independent in principle, but its *learned* parts are trained mostly on English and Mandarin, and degradation across datasets is measured (though that evidence concerns domain and channel, not language directly); we know of no figures for Taiwanese Hokkien or Hakka. Whether enhancement artifacts damage lexical tone is a reasonable prediction for which we have found no direct evidence. And the gap from Week 1 reappears: without public two-channel or multi-party conversational corpora there is no diarization or overlap benchmark for these languages.

## Learning Objectives
1. Write the microphone signal model of a full-duplex system (user, echo, competing speakers, noise) and, for each term, name the side information that lets us remove it — statistical difference, a known reference, a prior over speech, space, an enrollment utterance — and what happens when there is none (the permutation problem).
2. Formulate voice activity detection as a hypothesis test, state the cost of each of its two errors and of the hangover, place the hangover in the endpoint cell of Week 1's response budget, and explain why a VAD cannot answer "has the user finished?".
3. Formulate acoustic echo cancellation as system identification; derive the NLMS update and the bound $0 < \mu < 2$ from the principle of minimal disturbance; explain why double-talk breaks convergence, why the optimal step size is the ratio of residual echo to error, and which part of the echo a linear filter cannot remove (nonlinearity, delay jitter).
4. Write the Wiener gain and three masks (IRM, PSM, cIRM); describe how discriminative and generative enhancement each fail; use the orthogonal decomposition of the error (target / noise / artifact) to explain how SNR can rise while the word error rate gets worse, and why adding the observation back helps.
5. Derive the MVDR beamformer from a constrained minimisation, relate the distortionless constraint to artifacts, and explain the division of labour in mask-based beamforming (a network estimates the statistics, a linear filter does the removing).
6. Say what permutation invariant training solves and what it does not (output indices carry no identity), and compare blind separation, target speaker extraction and personal VAD as front ends for a dialogue system, including the case where the target speaker is not speaking.
7. Describe the embedding-plus-scoring architecture of speaker verification and its two errors; define the diarization error rate and show why collar and overlap conventions make reported numbers incomparable across papers; state the latency constraint on online diarization; and explain why "was that addressed to me?" is not an acoustic question.

## References
**Textbooks and overviews**
- **LOI** (Loizou, 2013; DOI 10.1201/b14529): in Part II, the chapters on spectral subtraction, Wiener filtering, statistical-model-based methods and noise estimation; in Part III, the two evaluation chapters (subjective and objective)
- **VVG** (Vincent, Virtanen & Gannot, eds., 2018; DOI 10.1002/9781119279860), Ch 3 (acoustics and the mixing model), Ch 5 (spectral masking and filtering), Ch 10 (spatial filtering)
- Hänsler & Schmidt, **Acoustic Echo and Noise Control: A Practical Approach**, Wiley, 2004 (DOI 10.1002/0471678406) — the standard text on echo cancellation: NLMS, step-size control, double-talk, and how cancellers, noise reduction and beamformers are ordered
- Haeb-Umbach, Heymann, Drude, Watanabe, Delcroix & Nakatani, **Far-Field Automatic Speech Recognition**, *Proceedings of the IEEE* 109(2):124–148, 2021 (DOI 10.1109/JPROC.2020.3018668; arXiv:2009.09395) — how the far-field front end (dereverberation, beamforming, separation) connects to recognition; the backbone reading for the second half of the week
- Wang & Chen, **Supervised Speech Separation Based on Deep Learning: An Overview**, IEEE/ACM TASLP 26(10):1702–1726, 2018 (DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2018.2842159) — the reference treatment of the masking view (training targets, architectures, generalisation)

**Voice activity detection**
- Sohn, Kim & Sung, **A Statistical Model-Based Voice Activity Detection**, *IEEE Signal Processing Letters* 6(1):1–3, 1999 (DOI 10.1109/97.736233) — a likelihood-ratio test plus hangover; the prototype of statistical VAD

- Zhong et al., **The Vulnerability of Neural Audio Watermarks under Speech Enhancement**, arXiv:2609.29040 (2026; preprint; cited in W9) — a side effect of enhancement on a different judge, the watermark detector
